blocks.text: Visible technique cards: what could each help?
Match each technique to a possible effect. These are options to explore, not ready-made personal challenges.
Point to a match and explain how the action could affect the work. More than one effect may be possible.
Then select an option that connects with your baseline. You may propose another safe arts technique with staff support.

items: A · Build tone through light, overlapping pencil layers.
B · Fold a small foot at the bottom of a paper shape.
C · Change the spacing of a repeated mark.
1 · A different visual rhythm across the page.
2 · A more gradual light-to-dark change.
3 · A form that can stand and be viewed from different sides.

blocks.text: Visible cards: find the useful check
Match each trial to a check that fits its purpose. Explain what you would look at rather than simply calling the work good.
Use these examples to practise the method. They are not a list of tasks everyone must place in their plan.
If a different check would better fit the artist's intention, explain your reason.

items: A · Try light pencil layers for a gradual tone change.
B · Test a folded foot on a paper form.
C · Compare two small arrangements of the same shapes.
1 · View from the side and see whether the form stands.
2 · Notice where the eye goes first in each arrangement.
3 · Look for sudden stripes between light and dark areas.

blocks.text: Visible trials: which answers the question?
Choose a card and keep your first answer ready. Point, write or hold its letter. Reveal your choice together, then explain your reason before hearing the adult’s model.
The adult wants to find what closer line spacing does. Compare these trial cards.
Which trial makes that question easier to answer? Explain what stayed steady and what changed.
The other trial may still produce useful art. It simply cannot tell us that spacing alone caused the difference.
Use this distinction when choosing what to test in your own work.

items: A · Same pencil, paper and light pressure; only the line spacing changes.
B · New paper, a darker pencil, harder pressure and closer line spacing.
C · Keep both trial patches and note the change beside them.
D · Rub out the first patch before there is a record, then write “better now”.

blocks.text: Sort these visible notes into ARTISTIC QUALITY, CREATIVE IMPACT, or NEEDS SUPPORT. Use the card numbers and explain a choice before we check.

items: 1. A slow opening pace gave the audience time to notice each movement.
2. The sharp contrast made me want to test pale shapes on dark paper.
3. It was good because it was good.
4. Repeated lines made a clear rhythm across the image.
5. I began to question how an empty space can become part of a work.

blocks.text: The key is ARTISTIC QUALITY: 1 and 4; CREATIVE IMPACT: 2 and 5; NEEDS SUPPORT: 3. These are sample notes, not claims about an event you attended.
At the actual experience, attend as an audience member. Follow the agreed access and conduct arrangements. Notice your chosen feature, then leave room for a detail you did not expect.

blocks.text: Match each card to ENCOUNTER, ORGANISATION, EDUCATION, CAREER, or INFLUENCE. These are example record types, not facts about a named person.

items: 1. My workshop sample and note name the artist, task and what I tried.
2. A checked page explains what an arts centre does and who can take part.
3. A provider’s course page explains the skills taught and entry requirements.
4. An artist explains a work route and the skills it involves.
5. I explain how a process I explored changes my next arts choice.

blocks.text: The key is ENCOUNTER: 1; ORGANISATION: 2; EDUCATION: 3; CAREER: 4; INFLUENCE: 5. Notice that education and career are separate questions, even where one route connects them.
At the real arranged meeting, meet the artist and join the first-hand workshop or event. Use your question when appropriate and keep the resulting evidence. Respect a request not to record.

blocks.text: Visible review cards: what is still needed?
Choose a card and keep your first answer ready. Point, write or hold its letter. Reveal your choice together, then explain your reason before hearing the adult’s model.
Read these example record types. Decide which could support a real review and which leave something important missing.
The cards are teaching examples, not statements about your own challenge. Explain what you would need to see or hear before accepting the record.
A review need not be long. It must concern the real challenge and give a clear view.

items: A · A general “looks great” comment with no link to the challenge.
B · Another person’s own view of the aim, changes and result, linked to the work.
C · An adult’s completed review copied into the pupil’s section.
D · The pupil’s own judgement of the actual process and outcome, with reasons.

blocks.text: Sort the visible cards into PROJECT AIM, MY LEADERSHIP ROLE, or NEEDS DETAIL. Think about whether the words explain a purpose or a personal action.

items: 1. Help learners explore texture through a shared collage.
2. I will show how to join two papers and invite learners to test the join.
3. My role is to do everything.
4. Give the group a way to choose and arrange work for a small display.
5. I will guide the choice of labels and check that each maker’s view is heard.
6. We will have a good time with some stuff.

blocks.text: The key is PROJECT AIM: 1 and 4; MY LEADERSHIP ROLE: 2 and 5; NEEDS DETAIL: 3 and 6. A useful role names something you can actually do and later review.
Improve one unclear card together. Keep the arts purpose and a manageable responsibility visible. You are practising a planning method before you write your own plan.

replacedWeDo.data-ta1: Every card and the key are provided. Gather individual choices before discussion. Do not replace the pupil’s later role with the class model answer.

blocks.text: Match these cards to PROMOTION, RECRUITMENT, RESOURCES, RISK, or FEEDBACK. Each card describes a practical planning decision rather than a completed event.

items: 1. A short message explains what the group will make and how to ask about joining.
2. I will use an agreed route to invite willing learners and check who can attend.
3. I will check the number and condition of the print tools before deciding the group size.
4. I will plan where wet work goes so it does not block the walking route.
5. I will ask learners to point to a choice in their work and say what helped them.
6. I will check that a grip aid and enough table space are available.

blocks.text: The key is PROMOTION: 1; RECRUITMENT: 2; RESOURCES: 3 and 6; RISK: 4; FEEDBACK: 5. A decision can affect another area too, but identify its main job here.
Which card would need revisiting if the group became larger? Explain a link between two areas instead of changing only one word in the plan.

replacedWeDo.data-ta1: Take individual responses before revealing the key. Accept justified cross-links after the main sort. All cards and their key are visible; no separate card pack is assumed.

replacedWeDo.data-ta1: Collect all sorts before giving the key. Accept speech, pointing or a marked letter; ask pupils to explain an action rather than judge a person.

blocks.text: Sort these visible cards into USEFUL TEST or NEEDS A CHANGE. Use the letter to show your choice before checking the key.
A: I ask a partner to try reading the task from the place they will sit.
B: I write that everyone understood before anyone tries it.
C: I ask what the partner found difficult and check I understood the reply.
D: I keep testing a damaged tool because the group voted to continue.
The key is useful test: A and C. B invents a result. D ignores a safety concern; stop and ask the responsible adult.
Choose B or D and explain a better next action. Keep the action specific. Saying communicate better does not tell someone whether to ask, listen, change the instruction or stop using a tool.

replacedWeDo.title: We Do · everyone commits
replacedWeDo.data-ta1: Read the cards aloud and collect each response. Separate helpful support from taking control of another person’s creative work.

blocks.text: Sort these visible cards into LEADERSHIP ACTION or NEEDS A CHANGE. Point to a letter and give a reason before checking the key.
A: I show the process on scrap paper, then let the participant try.
B: I say everyone joined in because their names were on my plan.
C: I ask what was unclear and change my explanation.
D: I finish their work without asking because time is short.
The leadership actions are A and C. B confuses planned participation with real participation. D takes away the other person’s action and choice.
Choose a useful replacement for B or D. You could record who actually took part, offer a smaller safe task, or explain which part needs more time. Keep the record honest when plans change.

replacedWeDo.title: We Do · everyone commits
replacedWeDo.data-ta1: Collect responses before giving the key. Do not infer personal needs, feelings or diagnoses from a pause or a question.

blocks.text: Match each visible card to OBSERVATION, POSSIBLE MEANING, or ACTION TO CHECK. Read the whole statement before choosing.
A: The person asked me to repeat the first step.
B: Perhaps they could not see where I pointed.
C: I ask which part they want shown again.
D: They paused after I moved the tool.
E: I demonstrate the move slowly and ask them to show the next step.
The key is observation: A and D; possible meaning: B; action to check: C and E. A pause can have more than one cause. We must not turn a guess into a fact about another person.
Choose one observation and suggest a respectful check. Keep your question about the task or access, without asking the person to disclose private information.

replacedWeDo.title: We Do · everyone commits
replacedWeDo.data-ta1: Read every card and collect each sort. Keep the discussion on actions and agreements, not labels for pupils.

blocks.text: Sort these visible cards under HELPS THE TEAM or NEEDS A CHANGE. Give your own response before looking at the key.
A: I check what my partner means before I answer.
B: I agree to a job without checking whether I can do it in time.
C: I explain that I need a different tool and agree a realistic task.
D: I change my partner’s section without telling them.
The helpful cards are A and C. B may leave another person relying on a promise you cannot keep. D changes a shared decision without a check.

Rewrite B or D as a useful next action. You could agree a smaller part, ask for support, or discuss a change before making it. The aim is a workable contribution, not a promise to do everything alone.

blocks.text: Sort the example review cards
Sort these cards under three headings: Judgement, Evidence, and Next step. All four cards belong to the paper-form teaching example. Write their numbers or point to a heading.

items: Card 1: “Moving the model made my explanation clearer for the person who asked.”

Card 4: “My project note records that I moved the model after a request.”

blocks.text: Compare one decision with someone else. Which card tells us what happened, and which explains what that event means?
Check key: Judgement has 1. Evidence has 2 and 4. Next step has 3. Evidence supports a judgement; the two are linked but do different jobs.

blocks.text: Match each record to the correct unit
Use two headings: Unit 1 — Arts practice and pathways; Unit 2 — Arts leadership. Match the four cards. Each is a labelled example of evidence, not a claim that you have completed it.

items: Card 1: A pupil’s action plan to develop their own drawing skill.
Card 2: A review of an arts event attended as an audience member, with evidence that the review was shared.
Card 3: A record of the pupil’s own leadership decisions while delivering the project.
Card 4: The pupil’s final review of their leadership project, using actual aims and feedback.

blocks.text: Check key: Unit 1 has 1 and 2. Unit 2 has 3 and 4. Card 1 belongs to the arts challenge. Leading a project cannot replace that personal arts-development work.

scope: Fourteen primary Silver activities plus concise teaching prose where measured load exceeded 1.25. Nine additional Bronze/Explore prose repairs bring this bounded batch to 23 revisions. Objectives, award allocations, nine-stage timings, practical stage 6 and printed requirements are unchanged; Silver 3005 independent instructions are restated without changing their requirements.
newFinding: The strict 1.25 finding is repaired and measured for all 42 routes, with unchanged medians and raw-ratio comparison.
proseReview: Worked methods, real practice, independent judgements and award requirements checked after shortening repeated explanations. Fourteen Silver activity revisions plus nine existing Bronze/Explore prose repairs: 23 units, zero new cells.
